grading_guide: Grade the behaviour of the code, not its style. Different names, formatting, loop types, if/else vs switch vs ternary, and helper functions are all acceptable when the results are the same.
Mentally run the student code on the question's example input and on boundary values (exact range limits, 0, empty input). Deduct only for inputs where the result is actually wrong.
A single small syntax slip (missing semicolon, one missing brace, a typo in one variable name) should not remove credit for otherwise correct logic unless the rubric requires runnable code.
If the question says return, console.log alone is weaker; if the rubric accepts display or return, both are full credit. Follow the rubric wording.
Do not give credit for code that only looks right: check operators, conditions, accumulation and the returned variable.
Code in another language than the one required should be flagged in review_reasons.

concepts.text: Function forms: function f(p) {...}, const f = function (p) {...}, and const f = (p) => {...} are all valid functions. An arrow function with an expression body (x => x * 2) returns that value without the return keyword. A function with no return statement returns undefined.
return gives the value back to the caller and ends the function; console.log only prints it and the function still returns undefined. Code after return in the same block never runs.

Integer conversion: Math.trunc removes the fraction; Math.floor rounds down (same as trunc for positive numbers, different for negatives); Math.round rounds to nearest; Math.ceil rounds up; parseInt(x), x | 0 and ~~x truncate. All return numbers. toFixed(n) returns a STRING. Number.isInteger only checks. JavaScript has one Number type, so 'integer' means an integer-valued number.
In JavaScript / is real division (7 / 2 = 3.5), there is no integer division operator; use Math.floor(7 / 2) for 3. % is the remainder and keeps the sign of the left operand (-7 % 2 = -1).

=== compares without type conversion; == converts types first (0 == '0' is true, 0 === '0' is false, null == undefined is true). '5' + 1 is '51' (string concatenation) but '5' - 1 is 4. typeof null is 'object'. NaN === NaN is false; use Number.isNaN.
Falsy values are false, 0, -0, '', null, undefined and NaN. Everything else is truthy, including '0', [] and {}.

let and const are block scoped; var is function scoped and hoisted (reads before the assignment give undefined). Reading a let/const before its declaration throws ReferenceError. const prevents reassignment but an object or array held in a const can still be modified.

for (init; cond; step) checks cond before every iteration. while checks before, do...while runs at least once. for...of iterates values of an array or string; for...in iterates keys (array indices as strings). break leaves the nearest loop; continue skips to the next iteration. Watch for off-by-one errors (< vs <=, starting at 0 vs 1).

switch compares with ===. Execution starts at the first matching case and falls through into later cases until break or the end. switch (true) { case cond: ... } runs the first case whose condition is true and is equivalent to an if / else if chain.

Arrays: push/pop work at the end, unshift/shift at the start (all modify the array). slice(a, b) copies indices a..b-1 without modifying; splice modifies. length is last index + 1. indexOf returns -1 when not found; includes returns a boolean.

map returns a new array of the same length; filter returns the matching elements; reduce((acc, x) => ..., init) folds to one value (without init it starts from the first element); forEach returns undefined; find returns the first match or undefined; some/every return booleans.
array.sort() without a compare function sorts as strings ([10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9]). Numeric ascending needs sort((a, b) => a - b); descending b - a. sort modifies the original array.

Strings are immutable; methods return new strings. split(sep) gives an array, join(sep) builds a string. str.length counts UTF-16 units. Template literals `${x}` insert values. s[i] and s.charAt(i) read one character.

obj.key and obj['key'] read the property named key; obj[k] uses the VALUE of variable k as the property name. Missing properties give undefined. Object.keys / Object.values / Object.entries list own properties.
Floating point: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. Multiplying by .5 or 1.5 on integers is exact enough for normal exam values; small float noise is not a logic error.

concepts.text: A recursive function needs a base case that stops the recursion and a recursive call that moves toward it. Missing or unreachable base cases cause infinite recursion (stack overflow).
Input validation (negative numbers, non-numbers) is only required when the question asks for it. Do not deduct for missing validation the question never mentioned; extra validation is acceptable.

A pre-computed constant equals the expression it replaces (for example 300 + 1800 written as 2100). Formulas with folded constants, reordered terms or extra parentheses are equally correct if the arithmetic is the same.
